newsitem.title: USA: Consumers and refiners squeezed by high oil price.
newsitem.headline: Consumers and refiners squeezed by high oil price.

text.p: Oil companies may again come in for criticism as gasoline prices turn up this quarter, but U.S. refiners are also being punished by the surge in oil prices in recent weeks, analysts said.

Though the major integrated oil companies lose on the refinery margins but make it up on the high oil prices, those in the industry specialising on the "downstream" end of the market are feeling the pinch.

"These are not the worst gasoline margins, but they are certainly one of the worst," said David Zinamon, director of refining and environmental affairs at consultants Petroleum Industry Research Associates.
Some of those companies heavily skewed toward gasoline refining are Chevron Corp, Valero Energy Corp Corp, Diamond Shamrock, Sun Co and Tosco Corp, analysts said.
The margin squeeze can be seen on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), where gasoline futures prices have lagged badly behind the 16 percent rise in crude oil prices since early August.
Thursday morning, gasoline's premium above marker West Texas Intermediate crude for October delivery fell to $2.25 a barrel, its lowest they've been since October, 1994.
The premium has averaged around $5 over the past two years.

The reasons for the dismal gasoline margins is that refiners have been increasing their runs to produce more heating oil, which has seen its premium skyrocket as inventories dwindled to historically low levels ahead of winter.

"They are going to try to lean toward making distillate (mainly heating oil) as much as possible but...for gasoline output this will be hard," said Linda Abramo, analyst with Energy Security Analysis Inc.
U.S. refineries generally are geared up to produce twice as much gasoline as heating oil from a barrel crude oil.

The pressure on gasoline margins is likely to remain in place for some months, made worse by the fact that Europe is facing a similar situation. With heating oil stocks there also running well below typical levels, European refineries also are producing a larger surplus of gasoline.
"We see maybe a little blip up (in the crack) in October or November to tensions between Iraq and the U.S. dying down , but we don't expect it to improve that much after that," said Abramo.
